scope: Fourteen existing Explore routes, unchanged canonical plan, part allocation, minutes and objectives. One primary native activity per lesson. Model answers concern stated examples, not grades on pupils’ artistic tastes. Real artist and arts group experiences remain required and unconfirmed unless the slot record says otherwise.

replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Read the four exact cards aloud as needed. Check all responses before giving the key. A pupil may indicate headings by pointing rather than speaking.

blocks.text: Use two headings: helps a planned line, and needs a change. Sort these cards by letter. The cards stay visible while you decide.

items: A: I try the route above the page before I draw.
B: I press harder each time I miss the edge.
C: I pause and choose where my line should end.
D: I keep drawing when the pencil grip hurts.

blocks.text: A and C help a planned line. B needs a change: pressing hard may make the mark darker, but it will not choose the route. D needs a change too. Stop and ask for a grip or tool that works for you.
Choose one card from the second heading. Say a useful next action. You might try a lighter touch, make space for your arm or ask for support. We change the action, not judge the person.

replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Keep all four statements on view and collect every pupil’s response before giving the key. Read or point through the model without supplying the pupil’s reason.

blocks.text: Sort these visible cards under two headings: a tone choice, and something else. Use the letters to show your answers.

items: A: Leave part of the paper white.
B: Make the sheet twice as wide.
C: Add another gentle pencil layer.
D: Turn the paper so your arm has room.

blocks.text: A and C change a tone choice. B changes the size of the paper. D changes how you can reach it. Size and reach can matter, but they are not the same as light and dark.
Choose A or C and say when you might use it. You could keep white for a light area or add a layer for a dark one. There may be more than one good reason.
Now point to the part of the model that shows your choice. Linking the action to its result will help your learning note later.

replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Keep cards visible and collect responses before the key. Change the actual tent’s spread after pupils predict; describe the observed result rather than requiring a fixed answer.

blocks.text: Sort the four visible cards under two headings: changes the form, and adds a drawn mark. Use each letter once.

items: A: Fold the paper back along a crease.
B: Draw a dark stripe down the side.
C: Open the two panels farther apart.
D: Shade a corner with a pencil.

blocks.text: A and C change how the paper sits in space. B and D add drawn marks. A sculpture can include both, but a drawn stripe alone does not make the sheet stand.
Point to the part of the tent that would change with card C. Say or show what you think would happen to its height. Then watch the teacher try it with the actual form.
We can make a prediction and test it. The test may surprise us. Use what the paper really does when you explain your learning.

replacedWeDo.title: We Do · everyone commits
replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Keep the full card set and both headings visible. Collect all pupils’ matches before reading the key, and accept a justified observation of interacting causes.

blocks.text: Sort these cards under two headings: check the join, and check the whole form. Match each letter to the problem it names.

items: A: The tape has peeled off the base.
B: The tab stayed attached, but the whole form tipped.
C: The tape touches the tab but not the form.
D: The base is narrow and the tall form leans.

blocks.text: A and C ask us to check the join. B and D ask us to check the whole form and its support. More tape is not the answer to every problem.

Choose a card and say a useful next check. For C, we could look for tape that bridges the two surfaces. For D, we could try a wider base position. The paper may behave differently, so test the idea before calling it a fix.

blocks.text: Visible cards: who could help?
Match these question cards to artist or arts group. Choose who you would ask first. Some questions may fit both; explain your choice.
Use the words on the board or sheet. You may point to the cards rather than read them out.

items: A · What tool made that line?
B · How do you help people try art?

replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Answer key: A/C preparation; B/D can evidence real exploration after they actually happen. A live screen is a route, not proof by itself; check the actual exchange.

blocks.text: Visible cards: preparation or real work?
Sort the cards into prepares me or can be real work. The second group only counts when the action actually happens.
Point to a card and say what lets someone take part. A screen can carry a live exchange or a recorded film. Those are different.
Keep the useful preparation cards. They can help you choose what to ask when a real session is ready.

items: A · Watch a film of an artist made last year.
B · Try a process with an artist during a live workshop.
C · Read a page about tools an artist uses.
D · Ask the artist a question in a live exchange and respond to the reply.

blocks.text: Visible cards: match the job and purpose
Match each job card to a purpose card. Use the words below, not a guessed story about the eventual group.
Could a job help in more than one way? Point to your best match and explain what makes it useful.
Keep these as possible roles. The real group may do different work. Find out through the experience.

items: A · Arrange pictures with space between them.
B · Set out safe tools for a workshop.
C · Invite questions about a piece of art.
1 · Help people think and talk about the work.
2 · Help people see each piece clearly.
3 · Help people try a way to make art.

blocks.text: Visible cards: what does this record show?
Sort these record types into preparation or a record of real exploration. They are example types, not claims that your activity took place.
Point to what would help you identify the person or group and your own action.
A record may need more context. A sample may have no label. What would help you find its source?
Use the sort to check your work. Keep a missing record marked as a gap.

items: A · A logo copied from a website before an activity.
B · A true note from a real artist session. It records the pupil’s question and reply.
C · Notes made only from an old film of a workshop.
D · A true arts group record. It shows the pupil’s action and finding.

blocks.text: Sort these cards into TEST, CHOICE, or FINAL WORK. Use the numbers on the screen. You can point, say the group, or write a letter beside each number.

items: 1. Two scrap prints show a light press and a firm press.
2. I will use wide gaps to make my path feel open.
3. The new collage is finished and all its pieces are fixed.
4. I tried rough paper and smooth paper with the same tool.

blocks.text: Check the key: TEST has 1 and 4. CHOICE has 2. FINAL WORK has 3. A test shows what happened. A choice says what you decide to do.
Do we have card 3 yet? No. We can keep a start today without claiming the work is finished. We will save the final piece when it is ready.

replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Every card and the key are visible. Cover or delay the key until everyone responds. Use the responses to check the difference between tests, intentions and finished work.

replacedWeDo.title: We Do · everyone commits

blocks.text: Sort these action cards into BEFORE GLUE, JOIN THE PIECE, or CHECK THE JOIN. The words are all here. Use each card number once.

items: 1. Try the small shape above and below the large one.
2. Keep a sketch or image of the loose layout.
3. Put a thin coat on the back, near the edges.
4. Press gently from the middle towards the edge.
5. Check whether a dry corner lifts.
6. Add a little glue under a loose corner, then press.

blocks.text: The key is BEFORE GLUE: 1 and 2; JOIN THE PIECE: 3 and 4; CHECK THE JOIN: 5 and 6. Talk through why saving the layout comes before fixing it.
A final photo alone would not show all these steps. Which card helps us keep a step that will soon be hidden? Card 2 does.

replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Collect an answer from each pupil before revealing the key. The visible cards can be sorted by number with no extra pack. Re-model glue use if the join sequence is unclear.

replacedWeDo.title: We Do · everyone commits

blocks.text: Sort these cards into KEEPS A BEFORE STATE or DOES NOT KEEP ONE. Think about what will still be there after a paper shape is covered.

items: 1. A clear photo shows the whole work before a new strip is glued.
2. A ring is drawn around an edge, then that whole area is painted over.
3. A separate sketch shows the layout before it changes, with the maker’s note.
4. Someone says, I will remember what it looked like.
5. The old test strip is kept beside the new strip.

blocks.text: The key is KEEPS A BEFORE STATE: 1, 3 and 5. DOES NOT KEEP ONE: 2 and 4. A memory can help you talk, but it does not keep the earlier work.
Which kept record could you use today? Choose a method that shows your real step clearly. You do not have to use a camera.

replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Take every pupil’s sort response before revealing the key. The cards are printed on the slide. Explain that a sketch and account must accurately show the actual earlier state.

replacedWeDo.title: We Do · everyone commits

blocks.text: Sort these record cards into PROCESS, FINAL WORK, or NEXT ACTION. Say or point to the group for each number before we check the key.

items: 1. A test strip shows the marks made with two paint coats.
2. A clear scan shows the whole finished collage.
3. A saved image shows the loose layout before its pieces were fixed.
4. I need to finish the last section before I record it as done.
5. My note says why I chose a small pale strip during making.

blocks.text: The key is PROCESS: 1, 3 and 5; FINAL WORK: 2; NEXT ACTION: 4. A next action is useful, but it is not proof that the action has happened.
Which two groups must be present for the complete Part C record? We need process and final work. Keep any next action honest until it is done.

replacedWeDo.data-ta1: Use the visible cards and key without an extra sheet. Gather all responses before revealing the key. Distinguish pending work from actual evidence without judging a pupil’s speed.

blocks.text: Sort the four example cards
Use three headings: Enjoyment, Achievement, and Needs a personal view. Point to a heading or write the card numbers beneath it. All four cards are here.

items: Card 1: “I liked the sound of the paper as I folded it.”
Card 2: “I made a base that held my shape up.”

blocks.text: Make your own sort first. Then compare one choice with a partner or adult. Which words helped you decide?
Check key: Enjoyment has 1 and 4. Achievement has 2. Needs a personal view has 3. Card 3 could gain a true personal view, but we cannot choose that view for its maker.

replacedWeDo.data-ta1: The complete example card set and answer key are on this page. Do not treat a pupil’s sort as evidence that their own sharing occurred.

blocks.text: Match the example records to the headings
Use three headings: Personal message shared, Preparation only, and Check the record. Sort these four complete cards by number. You can point or write.

items: Card 1: “I told my listener why I liked the rough marks.”
Card 2: “I chose a page layout but have not shown it yet.”
Card 3: “The note says I loved all the work. I did not say that.”
Card 4: “My listener read my page about the shape I was proud to make.”

blocks.text: Compare one match with someone else. What in the card shows whether the personal message reached a person?
Check key: Personal message shared has 1 and 4. Preparation only has 2. Check the record has 3; the note must match the maker’s actual view.
